scenes.text: Every time your phone opens a banking app, AES encrypts the traffic and the storage.
It was chosen in 2001 after an open international competition won by Rijndael (Daemen and Rijmen).

steps.title: Structure
steps.body: Block **128 bits**; key **128/192/256 bits** with **10/12/14 rounds**. The state is a 4x4 byte matrix. Each round: **SubBytes** (non-linear byte substitution from the inverse in GF(2^8) plus an affine map), **ShiftRows** (row i rotates left by i bytes), **MixColumns** (each column multiplied by a fixed matrix over GF(2^8)), **AddRoundKey** (XOR the round key). An initial AddRoundKey is applied first; the last round omits MixColumns. The key schedule expands the key into 11, 13 or 15 round keys. Not a Feistel cipher: all bytes change each round.

steps.title: GF(2^8)
steps.body: Bytes are polynomials with bit coefficients; addition is **XOR**; multiplication is polynomial multiplication reduced modulo **x^8 + x^4 + x^3 + x + 1** (0x11B). Multiplying by 2 (**xtime**): shift left; if the old top bit was 1, XOR with 0x1B.

steps.title: Solved: {57} x {13}
steps.body: {57}x{02} = {AE}; x{04} = {47}; x{08} = {8E}; x{10} = {07}. Since {13} = {01} + {02} + {10}: {57} XOR {AE} XOR {07} = **{FE}** (this is the worked example in the AES standard).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ordinary integer multiplication instead of the field's.
- Forgetting that decryption uses inverse operations in the reverse order (InvShiftRows, InvSubBytes, InvMixColumns).
- Believing AES-256 is simply 2x stronger than AES-128: both are infeasible to brute force; the larger key adds margin against future (quantum) attacks.

activity.prompt: Implement xtime and GF(2^8) multiplication (reduction polynomial 0x11B) and print hex of 0x57 x 0x13.

def xtime(a):
    a<<=1
    return a  # reduce when bit 8 is set
def mul(a,b):
    r=0
    while b:
        if b&1: r^=a
        a=xtime(a)
        b>>=1
    return r
print(hex(mul(0x57,0x13)))
activity.solution:
def xtime(a):
    a<<=1
    if a&0x100: a^=0x11b
    return a
def mul(a,b):
    r=0
    while b:
        if b&1: r^=a
        a=xtime(a)
        b>>=1
    return r
print(hex(mul(0x57,0x13)))

lessons.title: Lab: Modes of operation - ECB, CBC and CTR

story.title: The penguin that stayed a penguin

scenes.text: Encrypting a bitmap logo block by block with the same key (ECB) leaves the outline fully visible.
Chaining each block to the previous ciphertext (CBC) turns the picture into noise.

steps.title: Modes
steps.body:
A block cipher handles one block; a **mode** handles messages.
- **ECB**: C_i = E(P_i). Equal plaintext blocks give equal ciphertext blocks; leaks patterns. Never use for real data.
- **CBC**: C_i = E(P_i XOR C_(i-1)), C_0 = random **IV**. Sequential encryption; needs padding (PKCS#7); decryption parallel. A bit error garbles one block and flips a bit in the next.
- **CFB/OFB**: make a stream cipher from a block cipher.
- **CTR**: C_i = P_i XOR E(nonce || counter_i). Parallel, no padding; **never reuse (key, nonce)**.
- **GCM**: CTR plus a polynomial MAC = **authenticated encryption** (confidentiality and integrity in one). Always prefer an AEAD mode (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305). Plain CBC/CTR give no integrity: attackers can flip bits (padding-oracle attacks on CBC).

steps.title: Solved: toy 4-bit cipher E(x) = x XOR K, K = 0110
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reusing an IV with CBC or a nonce with CTR/GCM (catastrophic for CTR/GCM).
- Predictable IVs in CBC.
- Encrypting without authenticating.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone - stream ciphers and an LFSR keystream

scenes.text: A phone call has no clear block boundaries: a stream cipher XORs a never-ending keystream with the speech bits.
Hardware keystream generators were traditionally built from linear feedback shift registers.

steps.title: Stream ciphers
steps.body: C_i = P_i XOR k_i where k_i comes from a keystream generator seeded by the key (and a nonce). Fast, no padding, error does not propagate. Modern secure examples: **ChaCha20**, AES-CTR. **RC4** (once in WEP/TLS) has biases and is prohibited. A5/1 (GSM) is broken; never reuse a keystream.

steps.title: LFSR
steps.body: A shift register whose new bit is the XOR of tapped bits. An n-bit register with a **primitive feedback polynomial** has the maximal period **2^n - 1** (all non-zero states). **LFSRs alone are insecure**: Berlekamp-Massey recovers the register from 2n output bits; real designs combine several with non-linear functions.

steps.title: Solved: 4-bit LFSR, taps at bits 3 and 2, seed 0001
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Seeding with all zeros (stuck at zero).
- Using the same key and nonce for two messages: C1 XOR C2 = P1 XOR P2.

lessons.title: Modular arithmetic, Euclid's algorithm and Euler's theorem

scenes.text: It is 10 o'clock; 5 hours later it is 3 o'clock, not 15. Clocks add modulo 12.
Public-key cryptography is clock arithmetic with enormous clocks.

steps.title: Basics
steps.body: a = b (mod n) means n divides (a - b). Properties: (a+b) mod n, (a x b) mod n can be computed after reducing a and b. **gcd(a,b)**: largest common divisor; computed by **Euclid**: gcd(a,b) = gcd(b, a mod b). **a has an inverse mod n iff gcd(a,n) = 1**; the **extended Euclidean algorithm** finds x with a x = 1 (mod n).

steps.title: Euler and Fermat
steps.body: **phi(n)** = count of integers in 1..n coprime to n. For prime p: phi(p) = p - 1. For n = pq (distinct primes): phi(n) = (p-1)(q-1). In general phi(p^k) = p^k - p^(k-1) and phi is multiplicative. **Fermat**: p prime, gcd(a,p) = 1 -> a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p). **Euler**: gcd(a,n) = 1 -> a^phi(n) = 1 (mod n). **Chinese Remainder Theorem**: for coprime moduli m1, m2 the system x = a1 (m1), x = a2 (m2) has a unique solution mod m1 m2.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Computing a^b fully before reducing: use square-and-multiply with mod at each step.
- Applying Fermat when the modulus is not prime (use Euler, and check gcd = 1).

lessons.title: Lab: Extended Euclid and modular inverse

scenes.text: To decrypt, an RSA key owner must find d with e.d = 1 mod phi(n).
The extended Euclidean algorithm finds it in logarithmic time even for 2048-bit numbers.

steps.title: Idea
steps.body: Find integers x, y with **a.x + b.y = gcd(a,b)**. If gcd = 1 then x is the inverse of a mod b. Recursively: egcd(a,b) returns (g, x, y); if b = 0 return (a,1,0); else (g, x1, y1) = egcd(b, a mod b); x = y1, y = x1 - (a div b) y1.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Leaving a negative x: add n to bring the inverse into 0..n-1.

activity.prompt: Complete egcd and print the inverse of 17 modulo 3120.
activity.starter:
def egcd(a,b):
    if b==0: return a,1,0
    g,x1,y1=egcd(b,a%b)
    return g,0,0  # combine x and y
g,x,y=egcd(17,3120)
print(x%3120)
activity.solution:
def egcd(a,b):
    if b==0: return a,1,0
    g,x1,y1=egcd(b,a%b)
    return g,y1,x1-(a//b)*y1

lessons.title: Lab: RSA key generation, encryption and decryption

story.title: Locking with one key, opening with another

scenes.text: Anyone can drop a letter into a letterbox (public key) but only the owner has the key to open it (private key).
RSA (1977) does this with two large primes.

steps.title: Algorithm
steps.body: 1. Choose two large primes p, q; n = p q. 2. phi = (p-1)(q-1). 3. Choose e with gcd(e, phi) = 1 (commonly 65537). 4. d = e^-1 mod phi. **Public key (e,n); private key (d,n).** Encrypt: **C = M^e mod n** (0 <= M < n). Decrypt: **M = C^d mod n**. Correctness: e.d = 1 + k.phi, so M^(ed) = M . (M^phi)^k = M (Euler; also true when gcd(M,n) != 1 by CRT). **Signing** reverses the roles: S = H(M)^d mod n; verify with e. Security rests on the difficulty of factoring n.

steps.title: Real-world practice
steps.body:
- Textbook RSA is deterministic and malleable: always use padding (**OAEP** for encryption, **PSS** for signatures).
- Use at least 2048-bit n (3072 for long-term).
- Pick random primes; never share primes between keys (gcd attacks find them).
- RSA is used to transport symmetric keys, not bulk data (slow).

lessons.title: Lab: Diffie-Hellman key exchange and ElGamal

story.title: Two strangers agree on a secret in a crowded room

steps.title: Diffie-Hellman (1976)
steps.body: Public: prime p and generator g. Alice picks secret a, sends **A = g^a mod p**. Bob picks b, sends **B = g^b mod p**. Both compute the shared key: **K = B^a = A^b = g^(ab) mod p**. An eavesdropper must solve the **discrete logarithm** (find a from g^a) or the DH problem. Real groups: 2048-bit p or elliptic curves (X25519).

steps.title: Solved: p = 23, g = 5, a = 6, b = 15
steps.body: A = 5^6 mod 23 = 8. B = 5^15 mod 23 = 19. Alice: 19^6 mod 23 = 2. Bob: 8^15 mod 23 = 2. **Shared key 2**.

steps.title: Attacks and fixes
steps.body: Plain DH is **unauthenticated**: a man-in-the-middle can run one exchange with each side. Fix: authenticate the exchanged values (signatures/certificates, as in TLS). Use **ephemeral** keys (DHE/ECDHE) for **forward secrecy**: a later key leak cannot decrypt past sessions.

steps.title: ElGamal
steps.body: Private x, public y = g^x. To encrypt M: pick random k, send (c1 = g^k, c2 = M.y^k mod p). Decrypt: M = c2 . (c1^x)^-1. Randomised, so the same M gives different ciphertexts; ciphertext is twice the size.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Small p (< 2048 bits) or non-safe primes.
- Reusing k in ElGamal/DSA signatures: it reveals the private key.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone - primality, factoring and elliptic curves

scenes.text: An attacker has your RSA modulus n = 3233 and tries to break it by trial division. It takes a moment. With a 2048-bit n the same method would need more time than the age of the universe.
Generating keys needs fast primality tests, not factoring.

steps.title: Primality tests
steps.body: **Trial division** up to sqrt(n) is fine for small n only. **Fermat test**: if 2^(n-1) != 1 mod n then n is composite; but **Carmichael numbers** (e.g. 561 = 3 x 11 x 17) pass for all coprime bases. **Miller-Rabin** (probabilistic) writes n-1 = 2^s d and checks sequences of squares; error at most 4^-k after k random rounds. Real keygen draws random odd numbers and tests them (about ln(2^1024) = 710 candidates per 1024-bit prime, half that if only odd).

steps.title: Solved
steps.body: 97: 2^96 = 1 mod 97 -> passes (97 is prime). 91 = 7 x 13: 2^12 = 4096 = 45 x 91 + 1 so the order of 2 divides 12 and 2^90 = 2^6 = 64 != 1 -> composite. 561 passes the base-2 test although composite.

steps.title: Elliptic curves
steps.body: An elliptic curve over a prime field y^2 = x^3 + ax + b (mod p) has points forming a group; ECDH and ECDSA use scalar multiplication kQ, whose inverse (**ECDLP**) is hard. Roughly equal security: **ECC 256-bit ~ RSA 3072-bit ~ 128-bit symmetric**; smaller keys and faster. Curves: P-256, Curve25519 (X25519, Ed25519). **Quantum note**: Shor's algorithm would break RSA/DH/ECC on a large quantum computer; NIST has standardised post-quantum schemes (ML-KEM, ML-DSA) and migration is underway.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Fermat alone for key generation.
- Rolling your own curve or parameters: use standard ones.

lessons.title: Cryptographic hash functions and the birthday bound

scenes.text: Karthik downloads a Linux installer and the website lists a SHA-256 value beside it.
If even one bit of the file changed, the digest would be completely different. He compares them to detect tampering.

steps.title: Definition and properties
steps.body: A hash function H maps any-length input to a fixed-length digest. Cryptographic hashes need: **pre-image resistance** (given h, hard to find m with H(m) = h; work about 2^n), **second pre-image resistance** (given m, hard to find m' != m with the same hash; about 2^n), **collision resistance** (hard to find any pair; about **2^(n/2)** by the birthday paradox). Also: deterministic, fast, avalanche effect.

steps.title: Common functions
steps.body: **MD5** (128-bit) and **SHA-1** (160-bit): collisions demonstrated, do not use for signatures. **SHA-2** (SHA-256, SHA-512): Merkle-Damgard construction with a compression function; current standard. **SHA-3** (Keccak, sponge construction), different internal design. Password storage needs a **slow salted** function (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2, PBKDF2) rather than a plain hash. Uses: integrity checks, digital signatures, HMAC, Merkle trees (Git, blockchains), commitment.

steps.title: Birthday bound
steps.body: With n-bit output, the number of random inputs for about 50% collision chance is about **1.1774 x 2^(n/2)**. For n = 32: about 77,000 inputs; for n = 128: 2^64 (borderline); for n = 256: 2^128 (infeasible).

steps.title: Solved
steps.body: Daily classic: 23 people suffice for a 50% chance that two share a birthday (365 values): sqrt(2 ln2 x 365) = 22.5. For a 32-bit hash: 1.1774 x 65,536 = **77,163** inputs.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling hashing 'encryption': it is one-way, there is no key and no decryption.
- Using MD5 or SHA-1 for new signatures or certificates.
- Hashing a low-entropy password with plain SHA-256: GPUs test billions per second.

scenes.text: A device downloads firmware updates. A hash alone lets an attacker replace both the file and its hash.

steps.title: MAC
steps.body: A **message authentication code** T = MAC(K, M) gives **integrity and authenticity** (not non-repudiation, since both sides know K). Types: CBC-MAC/CMAC (from block ciphers), **HMAC** (from hashes), Poly1305/GMAC (fast polynomial MACs used in AEAD).

steps.title: HMAC
steps.body: **HMAC(K,M) = H((K XOR opad) || H((K XOR ipad) || M))**, ipad = 0x36 repeated, opad = 0x5C repeated, keys padded to the block size. The nested design avoids **length-extension attacks** that break the naive **H(K || M)** with Merkle-Damgard hashes (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-2). Compare tags in **constant time** (`hmac.compare_digest`) to avoid timing leaks. Also protect against replay by adding a sequence number or timestamp inside the message.

steps.title: Test vector
steps.body: HMAC-SHA256 with key 'key' and message 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog' begins **f7bc83f4**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- H(K||M) or H(M||K) instead of HMAC.
- Comparing tags with == in network code.
- Using the same key for encryption and MAC.

lessons.title: Lab: Digital signatures - sign and verify

story.title: The contract that cannot be denied

scenes.text: A vendor signs a purchase order digitally. Later he claims he never sent it.

steps.title: Principle
steps.body: **Hash-then-sign**: s = Sign(sk, H(M)); verify: Verify(pk, M, s) recomputes H(M). Provides **authentication, integrity and non-repudiation**. Schemes: **RSA-PSS/PKCS#1 v1.5**, **DSA**, **ECDSA** (P-256), **EdDSA/Ed25519** (deterministic, fast, recommended). Reusing or leaking the per-signature random nonce k in DSA/ECDSA reveals the private key (as happened to a console vendor). India's IT Act 2000 gives legal validity to digital signatures issued through licensed Certifying Authorities.

steps.title: Solved: textbook RSA signature
steps.body: Key n = 3233, e = 17, d = 2753. Pretend the digest is h = 2790. Signature s = h^d mod n = 2790^2753 mod 3233 = **65**. Verify: s^e mod n = 65^17 mod 3233 = 2790 = h, so valid. If the message is altered (digest 2791) the check fails.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Signing the raw message instead of its hash (and without padding): textbook RSA signatures are forgeable.
- Verifying only that a signature exists, not that the public key belongs to the claimed signer (needs certificates).

steps.title: X.509 and PKI
steps.body: A **certificate** binds a public key to an identity (subject), signed by an **issuer** (CA). Fields: version, serial, signature algorithm, issuer, validity (notBefore/notAfter), subject, subject public key, extensions (**subjectAltName**, key usage, basic constraints). **Chain of trust**: leaf -> intermediate -> **root CA** in the trust store. Browsers check: signature chain, validity dates, hostname match (SAN), revocation (**CRL** lists, **OCSP** online check, OCSP stapling) and **Certificate Transparency** logs. Public TLS certificate lifetimes are being cut steadily under CA/Browser Forum rules (from 398 days towards 47 days by 2029). **Let's Encrypt** automates issuance with ACME.

steps.title: Trust models
steps.body: Hierarchical CAs (web PKI) vs **web of trust** (PGP) vs private enterprise CAs. A compromised CA breaks trust for all its certificates: DigiNotar (2011).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring hostname verification.
- Disabling certificate checks in code ('verify=False') to make an error go away.
- Forgetting the intermediate certificate on the server (works in some browsers, fails in others).

scenes.text: Divya receives an OTP by SMS and, while on the phone with a fake 'bank officer', reads it out.
The OTP is valid, yet the fraud succeeds: authentication is about who and how, not only about what secret.

steps.title: Factors
steps.body: **Something you know** (password, PIN), **have** (phone, hardware token), **are** (fingerprint, face). **Multi-factor authentication (MFA)** combines at least two different categories. Phishing-resistant options: FIDO2/WebAuthn passkeys and hardware security keys, which bind the login to the real site's origin.

steps.title: Challenge-response and replay
steps.body: Server sends a random **nonce** N; client replies with H(secret, N) (or an encryption). A captured response cannot be replayed since the next nonce differs. Variants use **timestamps** (need clock sync) or **sequence numbers**. Needham-Schroeder (1978) key distribution using a trusted server was found vulnerable to replay of old session keys; Kerberos adds timestamps and lifetimes to fix it.

steps.title: Solved: password entropy
steps.body: A random 8-character password over 94 printable characters has 94^8 = 6.1 x 10^15 possibilities, about 52.4 bits (8 x log2 94 = 8 x 6.55). A 4-word diceware passphrase from 7776 words has 4 x 12.9 = 51.7 bits; 6 words = 77.5 bits.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- SMS OTP is better than nothing but is vulnerable to SIM-swap and social engineering.
- Using the same password on many sites (credential stuffing).
- Counting biometrics as secrets: they cannot be rotated if leaked.

lessons.title: Lab: HOTP and TOTP one-time passwords

story.title: The six digits that change every 30 seconds

scenes.text: Your authenticator app and the server both hold the same secret and the same clock.
From these they derive the same 6-digit code, with nothing sent over the network.

steps.title: HOTP (RFC 4226)
steps.body: **HOTP(K, C) = Truncate(HMAC-SHA1(K, C)) mod 10^digits**, where C is an 8-byte counter. **Dynamic truncation**: take the low 4 bits of the last byte as offset o; take 4 bytes from o, clear the top bit (mask 0x7FFFFFFF), then reduce mod 10^6.

steps.title: TOTP (RFC 6238)
steps.body: Replace the counter by **T = floor(unix_time / 30)**. The server accepts codes within a small window (+/- 1 step) to tolerate clock drift. Secrets are shared once, usually through a QR code.

steps.title: Test vectors
steps.body: Key '12345678901234567890' (ASCII): HOTP counter 0 -> **755224**; counter 1 -> **287082**. At Unix time 59 the TOTP counter is 59 // 30 = 1, giving the 6-digit code 287082.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Not limiting attempts: a 6-digit code has only 10^6 possibilities; rate-limit and lock.
- Reusing a code within its window (accept each code only once).
- Storing the shared secret unprotected on the server.

activity.prompt: Complete the dynamic truncation and print HOTP codes for counters 0 and 1 using the RFC 4226 test key.

def hotp(key,counter,digits=6):
    h=hmac.new(key,struct.pack('>Q',counter),hashlib.sha1).digest()
    o=h[-1]&0xf
    code=0  # 4 bytes at offset o, mask 0x7fffffff, mod 10**digits
    return str(code).zfill(digits)
k=b'12345678901234567890'
print(hotp(k,0),hotp(k,1))
activity.solution:
import hmac,hashlib,struct
def hotp(key,counter,digits=6):
    h=hmac.new(key,struct.pack('>Q',counter),hashlib.sha1).digest()
    o=h[-1]&0xf
    code=(int.from_bytes(h[o:o+4],'big')&0x7fffffff)%10**digits
    return str(code).zfill(digits)
k=b'12345678901234567890'
print(hotp(k,0),hotp(k,1))

story.title: One login for the whole office

scenes.text: A new employee types her password once at 9 AM and then opens email, file shares and the intranet without typing it again.
Behind the scenes Kerberos hands out time-limited tickets.

steps.title: Players
steps.body: **Client**, **Key Distribution Center (KDC)** = **Authentication Server (AS)** + **Ticket-Granting Server (TGS)**, and the **service server**. Every principal shares a long-term secret key with the KDC (users' keys are derived from passwords). Passwords never cross the network.

steps.title: Flow (Kerberos v5)
steps.body:
1. **AS-REQ**: client asks the AS for a **Ticket-Granting Ticket (TGT)**.
2. **AS-REP**: AS returns the TGT (encrypted with the TGS's key) and a TGS session key encrypted with the **user's key**: only the real user can decrypt it.
3. **TGS-REQ**: client sends the TGT plus an **authenticator** (client id + timestamp encrypted with the session key) and the desired service name.
4. **TGS-REP**: service ticket plus service session key.
5. **AP-REQ**: client presents the service ticket and a fresh authenticator.
6. **AP-REP** (optional): service proves its identity (mutual authentication).

steps.title: Why timestamps
steps.body: The authenticator contains the current time; the service accepts it only within about **5 minutes** of its own clock and remembers recent ones. A replayed authenticator is rejected. This is why Kerberos needs loosely synchronised clocks (NTP).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Clock skew greater than 5 minutes causes 'KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW' login failures.
- The KDC is a single point of failure and a high-value target: run replicas and protect it (stolen KRBTGT key = 'golden ticket').
- Weak passwords allow offline guessing of captured tickets.

lessons.title: Lab: TLS handshake, cipher suites and forward secrecy

scenes.text: A shop moves checkout to HTTPS. A security review asks which TLS versions and ciphers the server accepts.
You will probe the server with a simulated openssl client.

steps.title: TLS 1.2 handshake
steps.body: ClientHello (versions, cipher suites, random) -> ServerHello (choice, random) + Certificate + ServerKeyExchange (ECDHE parameters, signed) + ServerHelloDone -> ClientKeyExchange + ChangeCipherSpec + Finished -> server ChangeCipherSpec + Finished. **2 round trips**. Master secret derived from pre-master and both randoms.

steps.title: TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446)
steps.body: Removes weak options: only AEAD ciphers (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305), only (EC)DHE key exchange so **forward secrecy is mandatory**; encrypts most handshake messages; **1-RTT** handshake (0-RTT resumption possible with replay caveats). Cipher suite names are shorter, e.g. **TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384**. TLS 1.0/1.1 are deprecated; SSLv3 is broken (POODLE). In 1.2 a suite looks like TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 = key exchange, authentication, bulk cipher, hash.

steps.title: HTTPS hardening
steps.body: Redirect HTTP to HTTPS, **HSTS** header, valid chain, disable old protocols and RC4/3DES/CBC-only suites, OCSP stapling, short-lived certificates.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Certificates alone do not give forward secrecy: the key exchange must be ephemeral.
- Mixed content (HTTP resources on an HTTPS page) weakens the page.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone - IPsec, SSH and safe password storage

scenes.text: Two offices need to connect over the public internet as if on one private network.
An IPsec VPN encrypts packets between gateways; admins reach servers with SSH keys; user passwords are stored with PBKDF2.

steps.title: IPsec
steps.body: Operates at the **network layer**. **AH** (Authentication Header): integrity and authentication, no encryption (rarely used, breaks with NAT). **ESP** (Encapsulating Security Payload): confidentiality + integrity + anti-replay. **Transport mode** protects the payload between two hosts; **tunnel mode** wraps the whole original packet in a new IP header (gateway to gateway: site-to-site VPN). A **Security Association (SA)** is a one-way agreement with SPI, keys, algorithms; **IKEv2** negotiates SAs and keys using Diffie-Hellman and authentication.

steps.title: SSH and others
steps.body: **SSH** replaces telnet/rsh: key exchange, host key verification (known_hosts), client authentication by public key (disable password logins, use ed25519 keys). **S/MIME** and **PGP** sign and encrypt email. **WPA3** (SAE) improves Wi-Fi password handshakes over WPA2-PSK.

steps.title: Safe password storage
steps.body: Never store plain or fast-hashed passwords. Use a unique random **salt** per user and a slow **key-stretching** function: **PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256** (many iterations), **bcrypt**, **scrypt**, **Argon2id** (preferred). The salt defeats rainbow tables; the work factor slows guessing.

steps.title: Test vector
steps.body: PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256, password 'password', salt 'salt', 1 iteration, 32-byte output begins **120fb6cf**. Real systems use hundreds of thousands of iterations.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Same salt for every user, or no salt.
- Too few iterations or an outdated algorithm.
- Accepting an unknown SSH host key without checking its fingerprint.

print(k.hex()[:8],len(k))

courses.summary: Firewalls and iptables, intrusion detection, malware families, secure coding against SQL injection and XSS, wireless and network attack defences, and incident response with Indian cyber-law basics. Defensive and educational only.

lessons.title: Lab: Firewalls, DMZ and iptables rule order

scenes.text: A junior admin sets the firewall default policy to DROP while connected over SSH, before adding an allow rule for SSH.
Her session freezes and the server is unreachable. Rule order and defaults matter.

steps.title: Firewall types
steps.body: **Packet filter** (stateless): rules on IP, port, protocol. **Stateful inspection**: tracks connections (state table), so replies to allowed outbound traffic are automatically permitted. **Application proxy / WAF**: understands HTTP etc. **Next-generation firewall**: adds deep inspection, application ID, IPS. A **DMZ** (demilitarised zone) holds public servers (web, mail) isolated from the internal LAN by a second set of rules; internal hosts may reach the DMZ, the DMZ may not initiate connections to the LAN.

steps.title: Principles
steps.body: **Default deny** (allow only what is needed); **least privilege**; rules are evaluated **top to bottom, first match wins**; log drops; restrict management access to a jump host or admin subnet. NAT is not a security feature by itself.

steps.title: iptables essentials
steps.body: `iptables -L INPUT -n --line-numbers` lists; `-A` appends; `-I` inserts; `-m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT` allows replies; `-P INPUT DROP` sets the default policy. **Allow rules first, default DROP last.**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Setting default DROP before allowing your own session.
- Allowing 'any' to the database port from the internet.
- Putting a broad ACCEPT above specific DROP rules.

lessons.title: Intrusion detection, malware families and defence in depth

scenes.text: Files at a small clinic show a new extension and a note demanding payment.
Layered defences (backups, patching, mail filtering, endpoint protection) decide whether this is a bad day or a disaster.

steps.title: IDS and IPS
steps.body: **IDS** detects and alerts; **IPS** sits inline and blocks. **Signature-based**: known patterns (fast, misses new attacks). **Anomaly-based**: deviations from a baseline (finds novel attacks, false positives). **NIDS** monitors the network (Snort, Suricata, Zeek); **HIDS** monitors a host (logs, file integrity, e.g. OSSEC/Wazuh). Metrics: **false positives** (benign flagged) and **false negatives** (attack missed); **SIEM** correlates logs centrally.

steps.title: Malware
steps.body: **Virus** attaches to files and spreads when run; **worm** self-propagates over networks (WannaCry 2017 used an SMB flaw); **trojan** pretends to be useful; **ransomware** encrypts data for payment; **spyware/keylogger** steals data; **rootkit** hides presence; **botnet** = army of infected machines used for DDoS or spam; **fileless** malware lives in memory/scripts.

steps.title: Defence in depth
steps.body: Patch management, least privilege, MFA, email filtering and awareness training, network segmentation, endpoint detection and response, **tested offline backups (3-2-1 rule: 3 copies, 2 media, 1 off-site)**, logging and an incident plan.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Paying ransom as the only plan: backups should make it unnecessary and payment does not guarantee recovery.
- Treating antivirus as the only control.

lessons.title: Lab: Web application security - SQL injection and XSS

story.title: The login box that listed every user

scenes.text: A student project builds its query by pasting the typed name into the SQL string.
Typing ' OR '1'='1 turns the check into 'always true'. The fix is a one-line change: parameterised queries.

steps.title: SQL injection
steps.body: Occurs when untrusted input becomes part of the SQL **code**. Impact: data theft, authentication bypass, data destruction. **Prevention**: parameterised queries / prepared statements (data is never parsed as code), ORM used correctly, least-privilege database accounts, input validation as a secondary layer, error messages that do not leak SQL.

steps.title: Cross-site scripting (XSS)
steps.body: Untrusted data is sent to a browser as active content, letting an attacker run script in the victim's session (steal cookies, act as the user). Types: stored, reflected, DOM-based. **Prevention**: contextual **output encoding** (`html.escape`), template engines that auto-escape, **Content-Security-Policy**, `HttpOnly` and `Secure` cookie flags. **CSRF**: tricking a logged-in browser into sending a request; prevent with anti-CSRF tokens and `SameSite` cookies.

steps.title: Encoding
steps.body: html.escape('<script>alert(1)</script>') gives <script>alert(1)</script>: shown as text, not executed.

steps.title: OWASP Top 10
steps.body: The OWASP Top 10 lists the most critical web risks (broken access control, cryptographic failures, injection, insecure design, misconfiguration ...). Use it as a checklist.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Escaping quotes by hand instead of using parameters.
- Validating on the client only: attackers bypass the browser.
- Practise only on your own test database or a deliberately vulnerable lab you are permitted to use, never on real sites.

lessons.title: Wireless security and network-level attacks and defences

scenes.text: Rohan checks his bank balance on free cafe Wi-Fi with no password.
Anyone on that network can watch unencrypted traffic, and a fake hotspot with the same name could redirect him.

steps.title: Wi-Fi security
steps.body: **WEP** (RC4, 24-bit IV): broken in minutes. **WPA** (TKIP) obsolete. **WPA2** (AES-CCMP): secure with strong passphrases but PSK handshakes can be captured for offline guessing; **WPA3** uses **SAE** (a Diffie-Hellman-style password exchange) that resists offline guessing and gives forward secrecy; Enterprise mode uses 802.1X with RADIUS. Disable WPS, update firmware, use VPN on untrusted networks.

steps.title: Network attacks and mitigations
steps.body:
- **ARP spoofing / MITM** on a LAN: Dynamic ARP Inspection, port security, encrypted protocols (TLS, SSH).
- **SYN flood** (DoS): fills the half-open connection backlog; mitigations: SYN cookies, rate limiting, larger backlog, upstream scrubbing/CDN.
- **DNS spoofing**: DNSSEC, DoH/DoT.
- **DDoS**: anycast CDNs, rate limits, traffic scrubbing.
- **Port scanning** (reconnaissance): close unused ports, monitor with IDS.

steps.title: Solved: SYN backlog
steps.body: A server keeps 128 half-open entries for 60 s each. To keep the backlog full an attacker needs only 128 / 60 = **2.13 SYN packets per second**: tiny volume, which is why SYN cookies (stateless handling) matter.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Trusting a Wi-Fi network because it has a familiar name.
- Scanning or testing networks you do not own or have written permission to test: unauthorised access is an offence.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone - incident response and Indian cyber-law basics

scenes.text: An accounts clerk at a mid-size firm clicks a link in a fake courier email and enters her password. An hour later the mailbox sends odd messages.
The security team must act in the right order.

steps.title: Incident response lifecycle (NIST SP 800-61)
steps.body: **Preparation** -> **Detection and analysis** -> **Containment, eradication and recovery** -> **Post-incident activity** (lessons learned). Keep logs, preserve evidence, record a timeline, communicate through a defined channel.

steps.title: India: reporting and law (general education)
steps.body: The **Information Technology Act, 2000** defines offences such as unauthorised access and damage to computers (s.43/66), identity theft (s.66C) and cheating by personation using a computer (s.66D). **CERT-In** directions (2022) require organisations to report specified cyber incidents within **6 hours** and keep logs for 180 days. Individuals can report cyber-fraud to the national helpline **1930** and the portal **cybercrime.gov.in**. Cheating offences are also covered under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), in force from 1 July 2024. Personal-data duties arise under the **Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023**. This is general education, not legal advice.

steps.title: Containment first
steps.body: Disable the account or force a password reset and revoke sessions, isolate the device, block the malicious sender/URL, then investigate scope.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Wiping the machine immediately and destroying evidence.
- Hiding the incident: late reporting increases harm and legal risk.

scenes.text: Imran has one night before the cryptography exam.

steps.title: Classical and symmetric
steps.body:
- Caesar C = (P + k) mod 26; affine C = (aP + b) mod 26, 312 keys; Vigenere adds key letters cyclically.
- Hill C = K.P mod 26, det coprime with 26.
- Feistel: L' = R, R' = L XOR F(R,K); DES 64-bit block, 56-bit key, 16 rounds; AES 128-bit block, 10/12/14 rounds, GF(2^8) mod x^8+x^4+x^3+x+1.
- Modes: ECB leaks patterns; CBC needs random IV; CTR never reuse nonce; GCM = AEAD.

steps.title: Number theory and public key
steps.body:
- gcd by Euclid; inverse by extended Euclid; phi(pq) = (p-1)(q-1); Fermat a^(p-1) = 1 (mod p).
- RSA: n = pq, e.d = 1 mod phi, C = M^e, M = C^d; sign with d, verify with e.
- DH: A = g^a, B = g^b, K = g^(ab) mod p; needs authentication.
- Key sizes: RSA 3072 ~ ECC 256 ~ AES-128.

steps.title: Hashes, MACs, protocols
steps.body:
- n-bit hash: pre-image 2^n, collision 2^(n/2).
- HMAC = H((K^opad) || H((K^ipad) || M)).
- Kerberos: AS -> TGS -> service; 5-min clock skew.
- TLS 1.3: 1-RTT, ECDHE only, AEAD only. IPsec: ESP (encrypt+auth), AH (auth only), tunnel vs transport.
- Firewall: default deny, first match wins. SQLi: parameterised queries; XSS: output encoding.

cards.back: Equal plaintext blocks give equal ciphertext blocks
HMAC resists length-extension; naive construction does not
Ephemeral (EC)DH keys so past sessions stay safe after key theft

scenes.text: Asha wants a tiny console tool that greets each new hostel resident by name.
She installs the .NET SDK, runs `dotnet new console`, and sees Hello, World! in seconds.

steps.title: Anatomy of a program
steps.body:
- `using System;` imports the namespace holding `Console`.
- A `class` holds methods; `static void Main()` is the entry point.
- Statements end with `;`, blocks use `{ }`.

Since C# 9 you may also write **top-level statements** with no class at all.

steps.title: Solved example: greeting
Build and run
steps.body:
- `dotnet new console -n Hello` creates a project.
- `dotnet run` compiles to IL and runs it on the CLR.
- `Console.WriteLine` adds a newline; `Console.Write` does not.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- C# is case-sensitive: `console.writeline` fails.
- Forgetting `;`.
- `Main` must be capitalised.

activity.prompt: Read a name and print `Hello, <name>!`

quiz.q: Entry point of a C# console program
quiz.why: A C# console program starts running at the Main method, which is declared static void Main().
Console.WriteLine prints the text and then moves to a new line. Console.Write prints without the newline.
The C# compiler produces IL (Intermediate Language), which the CLR's JIT compiler turns into machine code at run time.
C# is case-sensitive, so Name and name are different identifiers.

scenes.text: The canteen app stores price as int and loses paise.

steps.title: Value types
steps.body:
- `int` (32-bit), `long` (64-bit), `double` (64-bit float), `decimal` (128-bit, exact for money), `bool`, `char`.
- `string` is a reference type but immutable.

steps.title: var and const
steps.body:
