steps.title: Task-based async
steps.body: `async Task<int> GetAsync()` returns a Task. `await` pauses the method without blocking the thread until the Task completes.

steps.title: Patterns
steps.body:
- `Task.WhenAll(t1, t2)` waits for concurrent tasks.
- `Task.Delay(ms)` instead of `Thread.Sleep` in async code.
- `async Task Main()` is allowed.
- I/O-bound → async; CPU-bound → `Task.Run`.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
```
static async Task<int> Square(int x) { await Task.Delay(10); return x * x; }
int r = await Square(5); // 25
```

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- `async void` except for event handlers.
- `.Result`/`.Wait()` can deadlock in UI apps.
- Forgetting `await` → method continues before work finishes.

activity.prompt: Write `static async Task<int> Square(int x)` that awaits Task.Delay(1) and returns x*x. In `static async Task Main()` read two ints and print the sum of their squares using Task.WhenAll.
activity.hint: Task.WhenAll returns an int[] of results.

options: asynchronously waits without blocking the thread
quiz.why: await asynchronously waits for a task to finish without blocking the thread, so the thread can do other work meanwhile.
async void can't be awaited and its exceptions are hard to handle, so it's used only for event handlers.
Correct: Task.WhenAll.
Task.Delay waits asynchronously, without blocking the thread. Thread.Sleep blocks it.

lessons.title: .NET overview: CLR, GC and the ecosystem

scenes.text: A startup asks the student club: can one language do web, desktop, cloud and games?
.NET runs on Windows, Linux and macOS: ASP.NET Core for web APIs, MAUI for apps, and Unity uses C# for games.

steps.title: How it runs
steps.body: C# → compiler (Roslyn) → **IL** in an assembly (.dll) → **CLR** JIT-compiles to native code. The **CTS/CLS** let C#, F# and VB.NET interoperate. **BCL** = base class library.

steps.title: Memory
steps.body: Locals of value types usually live on the stack; objects live on the managed heap. The **garbage collector** is generational (Gen 0, 1, 2) and compacts memory.

steps.title: Ecosystem
steps.body:
- Modern .NET (5 onward) is open-source and cross-platform; .NET Framework is the older Windows-only line.
- **NuGet** packages, `dotnet` CLI.
- ASP.NET Core (web/APIs), Entity Framework Core (ORM), MAUI, Blazor.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing .NET Framework with modern .NET.
- Thinking GC frees unmanaged resources — use Dispose.

activity.prompt: Boxing demo: read an int, store it in an `object`, unbox back to int, and print `Boxed=<v> Type=Int32`.

quiz.why: CLR stands for Common Language Runtime, the .NET runtime that runs the code and manages memory.
NuGet is the package manager for .NET.
The garbage collector's youngest generation is Gen 0, where new, short-lived objects are allocated and collected most often.
The JIT (just-in-time) compiler turns IL into native machine code at run time.

questions.why: A finally block always runs, whether or not an exception happened, so it's used for cleanup.
NuGet is the package manager of .NET. pip is for Python, npm for JavaScript and gem for Ruby.
CLR means Common Language Runtime, the runtime environment of .NET.
A bare throw; rethrows the current exception and keeps its original stack trace.
int.Parse("abc") throws a FormatException, since the text isn't in a valid number format.
await Task.Delay waits without blocking the thread, so the program stays responsive. Thread.Sleep, Wait() and .Result block.
The using statement needs a type that implements IDisposable, so Dispose can be called automatically.

questions.q: Run two tasks and wait for both
questions.why: Task.WhenAll waits until all the tasks have completed, while WhenAny returns when the first completes.
async void is only for event handlers, since callers can't await it or catch its exceptions. Other methods should return Task.

questions.q: IL is compiled to native code by
questions.why: The JIT (just-in-time) compiler converts IL to native machine code when the program runs.
The garbage collector frees managed memory automatically but doesn't release unmanaged resources such as file handles. Use using or Dispose for them.

questions.q: Calling .Result on an async method from a UI thread may cause
questions.why: Calling .Result on an async method from a UI thread blocks that thread while the task tries to resume on it, which can cause a deadlock.

uni-cse-datasci.title: Data Science with Python
uni-cse-datasci.description: From raw data to defensible conclusions: Python and NumPy, pandas wrangling, exploratory analysis and visualisation, and the statistics behind confidence intervals and hypothesis tests — with Python code activities.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Python and NumPy for Data
courses.summary: Core Python data structures and comprehensions for analysis, then NumPy arrays: dtypes, shapes, vectorised operations, broadcasting, indexing and aggregation.
outcomes: Learners can use lists, dicts, sets and comprehensions to process records
Learners can create and reshape NumPy arrays and reason about shapes
Learners can apply broadcasting and boolean masks
Learners can compute aggregates along axes

scenes.text: A class teacher has 60 students' daily attendance as a list of records.
With dictionaries and comprehensions, Sana computes each student's attendance percentage in five lines.

steps.title: Choosing the structure
steps.body:
- **list**: ordered, mutable sequence — rows of data.
- **tuple**: immutable record — (name, marks).
- **dict**: key → value lookup in O(1) average — counts, mappings.
- **set**: unique items, fast membership — distinct cities.
- `collections.Counter` for frequency counts; `defaultdict(list)` for grouping.

steps.title: Comprehensions and built-ins
steps.body:
- `[x * 2 for x in xs if x > 0]`
- `{name: m for name, m in rows}`
- `sum`, `min`, `max`, `sorted(rows, key=lambda r: r[1], reverse=True)`, `zip`, `enumerate`.
- f-strings for reports: `f'{name}: {pct:.1f}%'`.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Count by city.** `Counter(r['city'] for r in rows)` → Counter({'Pune': 3, 'Delhi': 2}).

**Example 2. Group marks by branch.** `g = defaultdict(list); for b, m in rows: g[b].append(m)`; then `{b: sum(v)/len(v) for b, v in g.items()}` gives averages.

**Example 3. Top 2.** `sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1], reverse=True)[:2]`.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a list for membership tests on large data (O(n)); use a set.
- Mutable default arguments `def f(x=[])`.
- Modifying a list while iterating over it.
- Integer vs float division confusion (`//` vs `/`).

activity.prompt: Compute the average mark per branch and print the dict with averages rounded to 1 decimal, keys in sorted order.
activity.solution:
from collections import defaultdict
rows = [('CSE', 80), ('ECE', 70), ('CSE', 90), ('ME', 60), ('ECE', 75)]
g = defaultdict(list)
for b, m in rows:
    g[b].append(m)
avg = {b: round(sum(v) / len(v), 1) for b, v in sorted(g.items())}
print(avg)
activity.hint: Group with defaultdict(list), then average each list.

quiz.q: Fastest structure for 'is this id present?'
quiz.why: A set uses hashing, so checking whether an id is present takes constant time on average. A list must scan through the items.

quiz.q: [x*x for x in range(4) if x % 2 == 0] =
quiz.why: The comprehension keeps only even x (0 and 2) and squares them: 0² = 0 and 2² = 4, giving [0, 4].
The // operator does floor division, so 7 // 2 = 3 (an int). A normal 7 / 2 would give 3.5.
'banana' has three letter a's (b-a-n-a-n-a), so Counter gives 3 for 'a'.
A tuple is immutable, so it can't be changed after it's created. Lists, sets and dicts can be changed.

scenes.text: Converting a million Celsius readings with a Python loop takes seconds.
With a NumPy array, `c * 9/5 + 32` runs in milliseconds — compiled, vectorised code.

steps.title: Why arrays
steps.body:
A NumPy `ndarray` stores elements of one **dtype** (int64, float64, bool…) contiguously in memory. Operations are **vectorised** — the loop runs in compiled C — often 10–100× faster than Python loops.

Create: `np.array([1,2,3])`, `np.zeros((2,3))`, `np.ones`, `np.arange(0,10,2)`, `np.linspace(0,1,5)`, random: `np.random.default_rng(0).normal(size=5)`.

steps.title: Shape, reshape, axes
steps.body:
- `a.shape` e.g. (2, 3) = 2 rows, 3 columns; `a.ndim`, `a.size`, `a.dtype`.
- `a.reshape(3, 2)`; `-1` infers one dimension: `a.reshape(-1)` flattens.
- **axis=0** runs down rows (one result per column); **axis=1** across columns (one result per row).
- Transpose `a.T`; stack with `np.vstack`, `np.hstack`, `np.concatenate`.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** `a = np.arange(12).reshape(3, 4)` → shape (3, 4). `a.sum(axis=0)` → 4 column sums [12, 15, 18, 21]; `a.sum(axis=1)` → 3 row sums [6, 22, 38].

**Example 2.** `np.array([1, 2.5, 3])` has dtype float64 — ints are upcast. `np.array([1, 'a'])` becomes strings.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reshape to a size that doesn't match (12 elements → (5, 3) fails).
- Confusing axis=0 and axis=1.
- Integer overflow with small dtypes (int8 wraps around).
- Appending to arrays in a loop (slow; build a list then convert).

activity.prompt: Without NumPy, simulate a.sum(axis=0) and a.sum(axis=1) for a 3×4 matrix of 0..11. Print both lists.
activity.starter:
a = [[r * 4 + c for c in range(4)] for r in range(3)]
# col_sums = ...  (axis=0)
# row_sums = ...  (axis=1)
print(col_sums, row_sums)
activity.solution:
a = [[r * 4 + c for c in range(4)] for r in range(3)]
col_sums = [sum(row[c] for row in a) for c in range(4)]
row_sums = [sum(row) for row in a]
print(col_sums, row_sums)
activity.hint: axis=0 collapses rows → one value per column.

quiz.why: The shape is (rows, columns), so np.zeros((2, 5)) has shape (2, 5).

quiz.q: a has shape (4, 3). a.sum(axis=0) has shape…
quiz.why: Summing along axis 0 collapses the rows, leaving one sum per column. For shape (4, 3) that is shape (3,).
The −1 means 'work it out': 10 elements in 2 rows gives 5 columns, so the shape is (2, 5).

options: Loops run in compiled code over contiguous memory
quiz.why: NumPy runs its loops in compiled C code over contiguous memory, so it avoids the overhead of Python loops.
When types are mixed, NumPy converts everything to the more general type. Ints and a float give float64.

scenes.text: Rohit wants to subtract each column's mean from a 1000×5 matrix.
Broadcasting stretches the 5 means across all 1000 rows — no loop needed.

steps.title: Broadcasting rules
steps.body:
Compare shapes from the **right**. Two dimensions are compatible if they are equal or one of them is 1. Missing dimensions are treated as 1.

- (1000, 5) − (5,) → OK (means broadcast over rows).
- (3, 1) + (1, 4) → (3, 4) — outer sum.
- (3, 4) + (3,) → **error** (4 vs 3); use (3, 1).

steps.title: Indexing
steps.body:
- Slicing `a[1:3, ::2]` returns a **view** (shares memory).
- Fancy indexing `a[[0, 2]]` returns a **copy**.
- Boolean mask: `a[a > 50]`, combine with `&`, `|`, `~` and parentheses: `a[(a > 10) & (a < 20)]`.
- `np.where(cond, x, y)` chooses element-wise.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Standardise columns.** `z = (X - X.mean(axis=0)) / X.std(axis=0)` — shapes (n, d) − (d,) / (d,).

**Example 2. Clip negatives.** `np.where(a < 0, 0, a)` turns [−2, 3, −1] into [0, 3, 0].

**Example 3. Shape check.** (2, 3, 1) + (4,) → compare 1 vs 4 (OK → 4), 3 vs missing (OK), 2 vs missing → result **(2, 3, 4)**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using `and`/`or` with arrays (raises error) instead of `&`/`|`.
- Forgetting parentheses: `a > 1 & a < 5` is parsed wrongly.
- Changing a slice and accidentally changing the original.
- Row-wise subtraction with shape (n,) on an (n, d) array — reshape to (n, 1).

activity.prompt: Write broadcast_shape(s1, s2) for two shape tuples following NumPy rules; return None if incompatible. Print results for ((1000,5),(5,)), ((3,1),(1,4)) and ((3,4),(3,)).
activity.starter:
def broadcast_shape(s1, s2):
    # compare from the right
    pass
print(broadcast_shape((1000, 5), (5,)), broadcast_shape((3, 1), (1, 4)), broadcast_shape((3, 4), (3,)))
activity.hint: Left-pad the shorter shape with 1s, then compare dimension by dimension.

quiz.why: Broadcasting stretches each dimension of size 1: (5, 1) and (1, 3) both become (5, 3).
Shapes are aligned from the right: 3 vs 4 don't match and neither is 1, so broadcasting fails with an error.
Use element-wise & on boolean arrays, with parentheses because & binds tighter than comparison: (a > 10) & (a < 20).
A basic slice returns a view that shares memory with the original array, not a copy.
np.where(cond, x, y) picks x where the condition is true and y where it's false, so [True, False] gives [1, 0].

lessons.title: Aggregation, random numbers and linear algebra

scenes.text: Is the probability of at least one six in four throws more than half? Priya simulates it.
10,000 simulated games give about 0.518 — matching the exact answer 1 − (5/6)⁴ ≈ 0.518.

steps.title: Aggregates
steps.body: `mean`, `median`, `std` (population by default; `ddof=1` for sample), `var`, `min`, `max`, `argmax`, `percentile`, `cumsum`, `unique(return_counts=True)`. NaN-aware versions: `np.nanmean`.

steps.title: Random numbers and simulation
steps.body:
Use a generator with a seed for reproducibility: `rng = np.random.default_rng(42)`; `rng.integers(1, 7, size=(10000, 4))`, `rng.normal(0, 1, 1000)`, `rng.choice`.

Monte Carlo: estimate a probability as (number of successful trials)/(number of trials); error shrinks like 1/√n.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Exact vs simulated.** P(at least one six in 4 throws) = 1 − (5/6)⁴ = 1 − 625/1296 ≈ **0.518**.

**Example 2. Linear algebra.** `A @ B` matrix product; `np.linalg.solve(A, b)` solves Ax = b. For A = [[2, 1], [1, 3]], b = [3, 5]: x = (0.8, 1.4) (check: 1.6 + 1.4 = 3, 0.8 + 4.2 = 5).

**Example 3.** Sample std of [2, 4, 6]: mean 4, squared deviations 4+0+4 = 8, divide by n − 1 = 2 → var 4 → std **2**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting `ddof=1` when the question asks for sample standard deviation.
- Using `*` for matrix multiplication (it is element-wise; use `@`).
- Inverting matrices explicitly instead of `solve`.
- Not seeding simulations, so results can't be reproduced.

activity.prompt: Compute the exact probability of at least one six in 4 throws of a fair die and print it rounded to 3 decimals.
activity.starter:
# p = 1 - (5/6)**4
print(round(p, 3))
activity.solution:
p = 1 - (5 / 6) ** 4
print(round(p, 3))

quiz.why: Mean = 2, deviations are ±1, sum of squares = 2. Sample variance = 2/(n − 1) = 2/1 = 2, so the sample std = √2 ≈ 1.414.
The @ operator (or np.matmul) multiplies matrices. The * operator multiplies element-wise.
Monte Carlo error falls as 1/√n, so to cut the error 10 times you need 100 times more samples.
Setting a seed makes the random generator give the same numbers every run, so results can be reproduced.
np.argmax returns the index of the largest element. In [3, 9, 2] the largest, 9, is at index 1.

questions.q: Which structure maps keys to values?
questions.why: A dict maps keys to values. A list and tuple are ordered sequences and a set holds unique items.
x % 3 for x from 0 to 9 gives only the remainders 0, 1 and 2. A set keeps each once: {0, 1, 2}.
The array is [[0,1,2],[3,4,5]]. Summing along axis 1 adds each row: 0+1+2 = 3 and 3+4+5 = 12.
Align shapes from the right: (8,1,6) and (7,1) becomes (_,7,1). 6 vs 1 gives 6, 1 vs 7 gives 7, and 8 stays. The result is (8, 7, 6).
b = a[0:2] is a view, so changing b[0] changes the same memory in a. So a[0] becomes 99.
Indexing with a list (fancy indexing) makes a copy, so changing b doesn't change a. a[0] stays 1.

questions.q: Assertion: `and` works element-wise on NumPy arrays. Reason: Python's and evaluates truthiness of whole objects.
questions.why: The assertion is false: and doesn't work element-wise on arrays. The reason is true: Python's and asks for the truth value of the whole object, which for arrays is ambiguous and gives a ValueError. Use & instead.
Mean = 4, squared deviations 4, 0, 4 sum to 8. Population variance = 8/3 and std = √(8/3) ≈ 1.633.
Each toss has a 1/2 chance of tails, so three tails in a row have (1/2)³ = 1/8.
Multiply each row of the matrix by [1, 1]: 1 + 2 = 3 and 3 + 4 = 7. So the result is [[3],[7]].
Adding the two equations gives 3x = 6, so x = 2. Then y = x − 1 = 1.

questions.q: Case: a loop appends 1 million values to a NumPy array with np.append. It's slow because…
options: Each append copies the whole array
questions.why: np.append makes a new array and copies the old one every time, so a million appends cost huge amounts of copying. Collect values in a list and convert once.
np.int8 holds −128 to 127. Adding 1 to 127 overflows and wraps around to −128.

questions.q: Which sorts a list of (name, score) by score descending?
questions.why: Sort with key=lambda t: t[1] to compare by score (index 1), and reverse=True for descending order.

questions.q: Case: Monte Carlo with 100 trials gives 0.47; with 1,000,000 trials 0.5183. Which is more reliable and why?
questions.why: The Monte Carlo standard error is about 1/√n, so with a million trials it is 100 times smaller than with 100. The law of large numbers makes the larger run more reliable.
X.mean(axis=1) has shape (500,), which broadcasts against the last axis (8) and fails. Reshape it to (500, 1), or use keepdims=True, to subtract row means.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Data Wrangling with pandas
courses.summary: Series and DataFrames, selecting and filtering, cleaning (missing values, types, duplicates), groupby–aggregate, merges and joins, reshaping and time series.
outcomes: Learners can load data and select rows/columns with loc and iloc
Learners can clean missing values, wrong types and duplicates
Learners can group, aggregate and pivot data
Learners can merge tables and predict row counts for each join type

scenes.text: The placement cell exports 2,400 rows: name, branch, CGPA, company, package.
With pandas, Ankita filters 'CSE students above 8 CGPA placed above ₹10 LPA' in one line.

steps.title: Core objects
steps.body:
- **Series**: 1-D labelled array (values + index).
- **DataFrame**: 2-D table of columns (each a Series) sharing a row index.
- Load: `pd.read_csv('file.csv')`; inspect: `df.head()`, `df.info()`, `df.describe()`, `df.shape`, `df.dtypes`.

steps.title: Selecting
steps.body:
- Column: `df['cgpa']`; several: `df[['name', 'cgpa']]`.
- `df.loc[row_labels, col_labels]` — by **label**, end-inclusive slices.
- `df.iloc[0:5, 1:3]` — by **position**, end-exclusive.
- Filter: `df[(df.branch == 'CSE') & (df.cgpa > 8)]`; `df.query("branch == 'CSE' and cgpa > 8")`; `isin`, `between`, `str.contains`.
- New column: `df['lpa_k'] = df.package / 1000`.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** With default integer index, `df.loc[0:2]` returns rows 0, 1, **2** (3 rows) but `df.iloc[0:2]` returns rows 0, 1 (2 rows).

**Example 2.** Top 5 packages: `df.nlargest(5, 'package')` or `df.sort_values('package', ascending=False).head(5)`.

**Example 3.** Count per branch: `df['branch'].value_counts()`.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using `and`/`or` instead of `&`/`|` (and forgetting parentheses).
- Chained assignment `df[df.a > 1]['b'] = 0` (may modify a copy — SettingWithCopyWarning); use `df.loc[df.a > 1, 'b'] = 0`.
- Confusing loc's inclusive end with iloc's exclusive end.

activity.prompt: Rows are dicts. Print the names of CSE students with cgpa > 8, sorted by cgpa descending (the pandas equivalent is a boolean filter + sort_values).
activity.starter:
rows = [
  {'name': 'Ankita', 'branch': 'CSE', 'cgpa': 8.7},
  {'name': 'Bilal', 'branch': 'ECE', 'cgpa': 9.1},
  {'name': 'Chitra', 'branch': 'CSE', 'cgpa': 9.3},
  {'name': 'Dev', 'branch': 'CSE', 'cgpa': 7.9}
]
# expected: ['Chitra', 'Ankita']
activity.solution:
rows = [
  {'name': 'Ankita', 'branch': 'CSE', 'cgpa': 8.7},
  {'name': 'Bilal', 'branch': 'ECE', 'cgpa': 9.1},
  {'name': 'Chitra', 'branch': 'CSE', 'cgpa': 9.3},
  {'name': 'Dev', 'branch': 'CSE', 'cgpa': 7.9}
]
sel = [r for r in rows if r['branch'] == 'CSE' and r['cgpa'] > 8]
print([r['name'] for r in sorted(sel, key=lambda r: r['cgpa'], reverse=True)])
activity.hint: Filter with a comprehension, then sort by cgpa with reverse=True.

quiz.why: iloc slices by position and excludes the end, so iloc[2:4] gives positions 2 and 3: 2 rows.
loc slices by label and includes the end label, so loc[2:4] returns rows 2, 3 and 4: 3 rows.

quiz.q: Best way to set column b where a > 1?
quiz.why: df.loc[df.a > 1, 'b'] = 0 selects rows and column in one step, so it modifies the original reliably. Chained indexing may assign to a temporary copy.
value_counts() counts how many times each distinct value occurs in the column.
df.info() shows the column names, how many non-null values each has and their dtypes, giving a quick overview of the structure.

scenes.text: The package column contains '₹12,00,000', '12 LPA', blanks and 'NA'.
Kunal strips symbols, converts types, treats blanks as missing and removes duplicate students.

steps.title: Missing values
steps.body:
- Detect: `df.isna().sum()`.
- Drop: `df.dropna(subset=['cgpa'])`.
- Fill: `df['cgpa'].fillna(df['cgpa'].median())`; forward fill for time series `ffill()`.
- Read options: `na_values=['NA', '-', '']`.
- Note: `NaN != NaN`, so use `isna()` not `== np.nan`.

steps.title: Types, strings, duplicates
steps.body:
- `pd.to_numeric(s, errors='coerce')` turns bad values into NaN.
- `pd.to_datetime(df.date, format='%d-%m-%Y')`.
- String methods: `s.str.strip().str.lower().str.replace(',', '')`.
- Categories: `astype('category')` saves memory.
- Duplicates: `df.duplicated(subset=['roll_no']).sum()`, `drop_duplicates(keep='first')`.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** '₹12,00,000' → remove '₹' and ',' → '1200000' → to_numeric → 1200000.

**Example 2.** Dates '03-04-2025': with `dayfirst=True` it is 3 April; without it pandas may read 4 March — always state the format.

**Example 3.** 5 rows, roll numbers [1, 2, 2, 3, 3] → `duplicated()` flags 2 rows; after dropping, **3** rows remain.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Filling missing values with 0 when 0 is a meaningful value.
- Ambiguous date formats (dd-mm vs mm-dd).
- Forgetting that operations return new objects unless reassigned.
- Dropping duplicates on all columns when the key is one column.

activity.prompt: Clean the package strings into integers; invalid or blank entries become None. Print the cleaned list.
activity.solution:
raw = ['₹12,00,000', '850000', '', 'NA', '₹6,50,000']
def clean(s):
    s = s.replace('₹', '').replace(',', '').strip()
    return int(s) if s.isdigit() else None
cleaned = [clean(s) for s in raw]
print(cleaned)
activity.hint: Remove ₹ and commas, then convert only if the rest is all digits.

quiz.why: df.isna() gives True for missing values, and summing the Booleans counts them per column.
With errors='coerce', values that can't be converted to numbers become NaN instead of raising an error.
NaN isn't equal to anything, not even itself, so np.nan == np.nan is False. Use isna() to test.

quiz.q: Remove repeated roll numbers but keep first?
quiz.why: drop_duplicates(subset=['roll_no'], keep='first') compares only the roll number column and keeps the first row of each duplicate.

quiz.q: Best fill for missing CGPA in a skewed distribution?
quiz.why: In a skewed distribution the median is a robust centre, not pulled by extreme values like the mean is, so it is a safer fill for missing values.

scenes.text: 'Average package and number placed, by branch and year — on one slide.'
Split–apply–combine with groupby and a pivot table answers it in seconds.

steps.title: Split–apply–combine
steps.body:
`df.groupby('branch')['package'].mean()`

- Multiple aggregations: `df.groupby('branch').agg(avg=('package', 'mean'), n=('name', 'count'), top=('package', 'max'))`.
- Group by several keys: `groupby(['branch', 'year'])`.
- `transform` returns a same-length result (e.g. each row's share of its group); `filter` keeps whole groups meeting a condition.

steps.title: Pivot and reshape
steps.body:
- `pd.pivot_table(df, index='branch', columns='year', values='package', aggfunc='mean')` — wide summary.
- `melt` converts wide → long; `pivot` long → wide (requires unique pairs).
- `pd.crosstab(df.branch, df.placed)` counts combinations.
- `cut`/`qcut` bin numeric values into ranges/quantiles.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Packages CSE [12, 8, 10], ECE [6, 9] → mean CSE 10, ECE 7.5; count 3 and 2.

**Example 2. transform.** Each CSE row's deviation from the CSE mean: 12 − 10 = 2, 8 − 10 = −2, 10 − 10 = 0.

**Example 3. filter.** `groupby('branch').filter(lambda g: len(g) >= 3)` keeps only CSE rows.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- `count` counts non-null values; `size` counts all rows.
- Forgetting `reset_index()` to turn group keys back into columns.
- Averaging averages of unequal groups (weighted vs unweighted).
- Using pivot (not pivot_table) with duplicate index/column pairs → error.

activity.prompt: Implement a groupby-mean and count: print a dict branch → (mean, count) in sorted key order.
activity.hint: Group values into lists with setdefault, then compute mean and length.

options: A Series the same length as df
quiz.why: transform('mean') returns the group mean for each row, a Series the same length as the DataFrame, aligned to the rows.

options: count ignores NaN; size counts all rows
quiz.why: In a groupby, count() counts non-missing values, while size() counts all rows, including NaN.
melt converts a wide table into long format, turning columns into rows.
The overall mean must be weighted by group size: (10 × 3 + 7.5 × 2)/5 = (30 + 15)/5 = 9. A simple average of 10 and 7.5 would give 8.75.
pd.crosstab counts the combinations of two categorical columns, making a contingency table.

scenes.text: Student details live in one file and fee payments in another, linked by roll number.
A left join shows every student and highlights who hasn't paid.

steps.title: Join types
steps.body:
`pd.merge(students, fees, on='roll', how=...)`

- **inner**: only keys in both.
- **left**: all left rows; missing right values become NaN.
- **right**: all right rows.
- **outer**: all keys from both.
- `indicator=True` adds a `_merge` column; `validate='one_to_one'` catches unexpected duplicates.
- `pd.concat([df1, df2])` stacks rows with the same columns.

steps.title: Time series basics
steps.body:
- Datetime index: `df.set_index('date')`.
- `resample('M').sum()` (monthly; newer pandas uses 'ME'), `rolling(7).mean()` moving average, `shift(1)` lag, `pct_change()` growth.
- `.dt` accessor: `df.date.dt.year`, `.dt.day_name()`.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Row counts.** Students roll {1, 2, 3, 4}; fees roll {2, 3, 5}. Inner → 2 rows (2, 3). Left → 4 rows. Right → 3 rows. Outer → 5 rows (1, 2, 3, 4, 5).

**Example 2. Duplicate keys multiply.** If roll 2 appears twice in fees, inner join gives 3 rows (2 twice, 3 once).

**Example 3.** Daily sales [10, 20, 30, 40]: rolling(2).mean() → [NaN, 15, 25, 35]; pct_change → [NaN, 1.0, 0.5, 0.333].

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Joining on keys with different types ('2' vs 2) → no matches.
- Unexpected many-to-many joins exploding row counts.
- Trailing spaces in keys.
- Forgetting to sort by date before rolling calculations.

activity.prompt: Given key sets, print the number of rows for inner, left, right and outer joins (unique keys on both sides).
activity.hint: Intersection, left size, right size, union.

quiz.q: Which join keeps all rows of the left table?
quiz.why: A left join keeps every row of the left table, adding matches from the right (or NaN where there isn't one).

quiz.q: Left keys {a, b}, right {b, c}: outer join rows?
quiz.why: An outer join keeps all keys from both tables: a, b and c, which gives 3 rows.
The rolling window of 3 at the last position covers 6, 9 and 12, whose mean is 27/3 = 9.
The string '7' and the integer 7 are different types, so they don't match in a merge. Convert the types first.
Percentage change = (new − old)/old = (75 − 50)/50 = 0.5, which is 50%.

questions.why: Each column of a DataFrame is a pandas Series.
iloc selects by integer position. loc selects by label.

questions.q: Filter rows where city is Pune or Delhi?
questions.why: isin tests membership in a list, so df.city.isin(['Pune', 'Delhi']) keeps rows with either city. The 'or' version isn't valid.

questions.q: df has 100 rows, 12 with NaN in 'cgpa'. df.dropna(subset=['cgpa']).shape[0] =
questions.why: dropna(subset=['cgpa']) removes the 12 rows with a missing cgpa, leaving 100 − 12 = 88.
pandas skips NaN when taking a mean, so the mean of 5 and 7 is 6.
count() counts only non-missing values (2), while size counts all entries including NaN (3).

questions.q: Assertion: Averaging group averages always equals the overall mean. Reason: Groups can have different sizes.
questions.why: The assertion is false: the mean of group means equals the overall mean only if the groups are equal in size. The reason is true, since groups can have different sizes, which is why a weighted average is needed.

questions.q: Left table 5 unique keys; right table has each key twice. Inner join rows?
questions.why: Each of the 5 left keys matches 2 rows on the right, so the inner join gives 5 × 2 = 10 rows.

questions.q: Students {1..6}, results {4..9}: left join rows (unique keys)?
questions.why: A left join keeps every row from the left table: students 1 to 6, so 6 rows, with missing results for those without a match.

questions.q: Which reshapes columns Jan, Feb, Mar into rows (month, value)?
questions.why: melt turns the columns Jan, Feb and Mar into rows with a month and value, converting wide data to long.

questions.q: Case: after a merge, row count jumps from 10,000 to 85,000. Likely cause?
questions.why: A jump in rows after a merge usually means duplicate keys on both sides, giving many-to-many matches. Check the keys, or use validate= in merge.

questions.q: Why does df[df.a > 0]['b'] = 1 sometimes not change df?
options: It may assign to a temporary copy
questions.why: df[df.a > 0]['b'] = 1 first makes a temporary filtered DataFrame and assigns into that, so the original may not change. Use df.loc[mask, 'b'] = 1.
shift(1) moves the values down by one position, so the first becomes NaN: [NaN, 10, 20].

questions.q: Case: '05-06-2025' parsed as 6 May but meant 5 June. Fix?
questions.why: By default 05-06-2025 may be read as month-first. Give an explicit format, '%d-%m-%Y', or dayfirst=True, to read it as 5 June.

options: All rows of departments whose mean salary > 50
questions.why: filter on a groupby keeps all rows of the groups for which the function returns True, so departments whose mean salary is above 50.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Exploratory Data Analysis and Visualisation
courses.summary: Descriptive statistics, distributions and outliers, relationships and correlation, choosing the right chart, matplotlib/seaborn basics and honest data storytelling.
outcomes: Learners can summarise data with centre, spread and shape
Learners can detect outliers with IQR and z-scores
Learners can compute and interpret correlation without confusing it with causation
Learners can choose and critique charts for a message

scenes.text: A start-up advertises an 'average salary of ₹25 LPA'. Most employees earn ₹6–8 LPA.
The two founders' huge salaries pull the mean up; the median tells the real story.

steps.title: Centre and spread
steps.body:
- **Mean** (sensitive to outliers), **median** (robust), **mode** (most frequent).
- **Range**, **variance**, **standard deviation**, **IQR** = Q3 − Q1 (robust).
- Percentiles: the p-th percentile has p% of values below it.

steps.title: Shape
steps.body:
- **Right (positive) skew**: long tail to the right; mean > median (incomes, house prices).
- **Left skew**: mean < median (marks in an easy exam).
- Symmetric: mean ≈ median.
- **Kurtosis**: heaviness of tails.
- Bimodal distributions often hide two groups — split them.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Salaries (LPA) [6, 7, 7, 8, 8, 90, 120]: mean = 246/7 ≈ **35.1**; median = **8**. Report the median.

**Example 2. Quartiles** of [2, 4, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10, 12] (median-of-halves method): Q1 = median(2, 4, 4, 5) = 4, Q3 = median(7, 9, 10, 12) = 9.5 → IQR = **5.5**. (Software may use interpolation and give slightly different values.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reporting the mean for skewed data.
- Forgetting that different quartile methods give different answers — state the method.
- Ignoring units.
- Summarising bimodal data with one number.

activity.prompt: Print the mean (1 decimal) and median of the salary list.
activity.starter:
s = [6, 7, 7, 8, 8, 90, 120]
# mean, median
print(round(mean, 1), median)
activity.solution:
s = [6, 7, 7, 8, 8, 90, 120]
mean = sum(s) / len(s)
t = sorted(s)
n = len(t)
median = t[n // 2] if n % 2 else (t[n // 2 - 1] + t[n // 2]) / 2
print(round(mean, 1), median)
activity.hint: Sort for the median; odd length → middle element.

quiz.why: In right-skewed data a few large values pull the mean up above the median, so mean > median.
The interquartile range (IQR) uses only the middle 50% of the data, so extreme values hardly affect it.
Sort the values: 1, 1, 3, 4, 5. The middle one is 3.
With an even number of values, the median is the average of the two middle ones: (4 + 6)/2 = 5.
Two peaks (bimodal) often mean two different groups are mixed in the data, so look into splitting them.

scenes.text: A hospital dataset shows a patient aged 250 and another with height 17 cm.
EDA catches data-entry errors before they ruin the model.

steps.title: Detection methods
steps.body:
- **IQR rule**: outside [Q1 − 1.5·IQR, Q3 + 1.5·IQR] (box plot whiskers).
- **z-score**: |z| > 3 for roughly normal data.
- Domain rules: age 0–120, percentages 0–100.
- Visual: box plots, histograms, scatter plots.

steps.title: What to do
steps.body:
- Data error → fix from source or set to missing.
- Genuine extreme → keep; use robust statistics, log transform, or cap (winsorise) with justification.
- Always document the decision; never delete inconvenient points silently.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Q1 = 30, Q3 = 50 → IQR 20 → fences 0 and 80. Values 85 and −5 are outliers.

**Example 2.** Mean 60, std 8 → z(90) = 3.75 → flag.

**Example 3. Log transform.** Incomes 1, 10, 100 lakh become log₁₀: 0, 1, 2 — evenly spaced, tail compressed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using z-scores on very skewed data (the outlier inflates the std and hides itself).
- Removing outliers before understanding them (they may be the fraud you want).
- Applying rules computed on the full dataset before the train/test split.

activity.prompt: Given Q1 = 30 and Q3 = 50, print the values outside the IQR fences.
activity.starter:
vals = [-5, 12, 30, 45, 50, 79, 85]
q1, q3 = 30, 50
# print outliers list
activity.solution:
vals = [-5, 12, 30, 45, 50, 79, 85]
q1, q3 = 30, 50
iqr = q3 - q1
lo, hi = q1 - 1.5 * iqr, q3 + 1.5 * iqr
print([v for v in vals if v < lo or v > hi])

quiz.why: IQR = 20 − 10 = 10. The upper fence is Q3 + 1.5 × IQR = 20 + 15 = 35.
A common rule flags values with |z| > 3 as outliers, as they're rare under a normal distribution.

quiz.q: A genuine but extreme value should usually be…
options: Kept and handled with robust methods or transforms
quiz.why: A genuine extreme value is real data, so it should be kept. Use robust methods or a transform such as a log to handle it.
log₁₀ 1000 = 3, since 10³ = 1000.

quiz.q: Box plot whiskers usually extend to…
quiz.why: Box plot whiskers by Tukey's rule extend to the furthest data within 1.5 × IQR beyond the quartiles. Points beyond are shown as outliers.

scenes.text: A newspaper notices ice-cream sales and drowning incidents rise together.
The hidden cause is summer heat — a confounder. Correlation is not causation.

steps.title: Pearson and Spearman
steps.body:
**Pearson r = cov(X, Y)/(σ_X σ_Y)**, in [−1, 1], measures **linear** association. r² is the fraction of variance explained by a linear fit.

**Spearman ρ** = Pearson on ranks — captures monotonic relationships and is robust to outliers.

r = 0 does **not** mean no relationship (e.g. y = x² on symmetric x).

steps.title: Causation pitfalls
steps.body:
- **Confounding**: a third variable drives both.
- **Reverse causation**.
- **Selection bias**.
- **Simpson's paradox**: a trend in each group reverses when groups are combined.
- Randomised experiments (A/B tests) are the gold standard for causal claims.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** x = [1, 2, 3], y = [2, 4, 6]: perfectly linear → **r = 1**.

**Example 2.** x = [−2, −1, 0, 1, 2], y = x² = [4, 1, 0, 1, 4]: cov = 0 → **r = 0** despite a perfect relationship.

**Example 3. Simpson.** Treatment A cures 81/87 small stones (93%) and 192/263 large (73%); B cures 234/270 small (87%) and 55/80 large (69%). A is better in both groups, but overall A = 273/350 (78%) vs B = 289/350 (83%) — because A was given the harder cases more often.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Claiming causation from observational correlation.
- Using Pearson for curved or outlier-heavy data.
- Ignoring group structure (Simpson's paradox).
- Reading r = 0.3 as '30% caused'.

activity.prompt: Write pearson(x, y) and print r for ([1,2,3],[2,4,6]) and for ([-2,-1,0,1,2],[4,1,0,1,4]) rounded to 2 decimals.
activity.starter:
import math
def pearson(x, y):
    # cov / (sx * sy)
    pass
print(round(pearson([1,2,3],[2,4,6]), 2), round(pearson([-2,-1,0,1,2],[4,1,0,1,4]), 2))
activity.solution:
import math
def pearson(x, y):
    mx, my = sum(x) / len(x), sum(y) / len(y)
    cov = sum((a - mx) * (b - my) for a, b in zip(x, y))
    sx = math.sqrt(sum((a - mx) ** 2 for a in x))
    sy = math.sqrt(sum((b - my) ** 2 for b in y))
    return cov / (sx * sy)
print(round(pearson([1,2,3],[2,4,6]), 2), round(pearson([-2,-1,0,1,2],[4,1,0,1,4]), 2))
activity.hint: The n factors cancel; use sums of deviations.

quiz.why: r = −0.9 is close to −1, so there is a strong negative linear relationship. It does not prove one variable causes the other.
r = 0 means no linear relationship. A strong non-linear relationship can still exist.
Spearman correlation is Pearson correlation applied to the ranks of the data, so it measures monotonic relationships and resists outliers.

quiz.q: A third variable driving both X and Y is a…
quiz.why: A confounder is a third variable that influences both X and Y, which can make them look related when they aren't directly.
r² = 0.8² = 0.64, so about 64% of the variance is explained by the linear relationship.

scenes.text: A bar chart makes a 2% rise look like a doubling — its y-axis starts at 98.
Redrawn from zero with clear labels, the honest story is 'a small improvement'.

steps.title: Chart by question
steps.body:
- Compare categories → **bar chart** (start at 0).
- Trend over time → **line chart**.
- Distribution → **histogram**, box plot, violin.
- Relationship → **scatter plot** (add trend line; colour by group).
- Part of whole → stacked bar (pie only for 2–3 parts).
- Many variables → heatmap of correlations, small multiples.

steps.title: matplotlib / seaborn basics
steps.body:
`fig, ax = plt.subplots(); ax.bar(x, y); ax.set_title('...'); ax.set_xlabel('...'); ax.set_ylabel('... (units)')`.

seaborn: `sns.histplot(df, x='cgpa', hue='branch')`, `sns.boxplot`, `sns.scatterplot`, `sns.heatmap(df.corr(numeric_only=True), annot=True)`.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Truncated axis.** Values 98 and 100 drawn from an axis starting at 97: bars of height 1 and 3 — visually **3×** for a 2% difference.

**Example 2. Choose.** 'How did monthly active users change in 2025?' → line chart. 'Which branch has the most placements?' → sorted bar chart.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Bar charts not starting at zero; dual axes that imply false correlations.
- 3-D and pie charts with many slices.
- Missing units, titles or sources.
- Red/green-only colour coding (colour-blind readers); use colour-blind-safe palettes.

activity.prompt: Match the question to the best chart.

quiz.why: Bar length encodes value, so bars should start at zero. Otherwise the differences look larger than they are.

quiz.q: Best for showing a distribution's outliers?
quiz.why: A box plot shows the median, quartiles and outliers of a distribution, so it is good for spotting outliers.

quiz.q: Values 50 and 51 with axis starting at 49: visual ratio?
quiz.why: With the axis starting at 49, the bars have heights 1 and 2, so the 51 bar looks twice as tall, although it's only 2% bigger. The truncated axis exaggerates the difference.
Use colour-blind-safe palettes and add labels or patterns, so people with colour-vision differences can read the chart. Red versus green is hard for many.
Pie charts work only for 2–3 parts of a whole. With more slices, people can't compare the angles well.

questions.why: The median is the most robust measure of centre, because extreme values don't move it much. The mean is pulled by outliers.
In left-skewed data the long tail on the left pulls the mean below the median, so mean < median.
IQR = 18 − 12 = 6. The lower fence is Q1 − 1.5 × IQR = 12 − 9 = 3.

questions.q: Assertion: Pearson r near 0 proves X and Y are independent. Reason: Pearson measures only linear association.
questions.why: The assertion is false: Pearson r near 0 doesn't prove independence, since variables can have a strong non-linear dependence. The reason is true: Pearson measures only linear association.
The points lie exactly on a straight line going down: y = 10 − 2x. When all points fall on a perfect negative line, Pearson r = −1.

questions.q: Case: cities with more hospitals have more deaths. Most likely explanation?
questions.why: Big cities have both more hospitals and more deaths, since they have more people. Population size is a confounder driving both counts, so the link doesn't show hospitals cause deaths.

options: A trend within groups reverses when groups are combined
questions.why: Simpson's paradox is when a trend that appears in every group reverses (or disappears) once the groups are combined, usually because the groups differ in size or composition.

questions.q: Chart for comparing exam score distributions of 4 sections?
questions.why: Side-by-side box plots show the median, spread and outliers of each section, so the four distributions can be compared easily.

questions.q: Why can z-scores fail to flag an extreme outlier in small data?
options: The outlier inflates the std itself
questions.why: In a small sample an extreme outlier inflates the standard deviation itself, so its own z-score stays modest and may be missed. This is the masking effect.
The mean is (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 100)/5 = 110/5 = 22. The median is the middle value, 3. The outlier pulls the mean far away but not the median.

questions.q: Case: a dashboard bar chart starts its y-axis at 950 for values 960 and 990. Problem?
questions.why: Starting the axis at 950 makes the 960 bar look tiny and the 990 bar look huge, so a small difference seems large. Bars should start at 0.

questions.q: r = 0.5 means the linear model explains what share of variance?
questions.why: The share of variance explained by a linear model is r² = 0.5² = 0.25, or 25%.

questions.q: Case: A is better than B in both age groups, but B looks better overall. Which statement is right?
options: Group sizes/assignment differ — analyse stratified results
questions.why: When A is better in each age group but B looks better overall, it's Simpson's paradox. The groups differ in size or assignment, so analyse the results stratified by group instead of using the overall figure.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Probability, Inference and Hypothesis Testing
courses.summary: Probability rules and Bayes, common distributions, sampling and the central limit theorem, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests (z, t, chi-square), p-values, errors and A/B testing.
outcomes: Learners can apply probability rules and Bayes' theorem
Learners can use binomial, Poisson and normal distributions
Learners can build confidence intervals using the CLT
Learners can run and interpret z/t/chi-square tests and design A/B tests

scenes.text: A test is 99% sensitive and 95% specific. Rare disease: 1 in 100 people. Arjun tests positive and panics.
Bayes shows the chance he actually has it is only about 17% — confirmatory testing is needed.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
- P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)
- Conditional P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B)
- Independence: P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B)
- Total probability: P(B) = Σ P(B | Aᵢ)P(Aᵢ)
- **Bayes: P(A | B) = P(B | A)P(A)/P(B)**

steps.title: Think in counts
steps.body: Converting probabilities into 'out of 10,000 people' makes Bayes problems intuitive and is a great way to check answers.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing P(+|D) with P(D|+) (the prosecutor's fallacy).
- Ignoring the base rate.
- Adding probabilities of overlapping events without subtracting the intersection.
- Assuming independence without justification.

activity.prompt: Compute P(D | +) for prevalence 0.01, sensitivity 0.99, false positive rate 0.05. Print rounded to 3 decimals.
activity.starter:
p_d, sens, fpr = 0.01, 0.99, 0.05
# post = ...
print(round(post, 3))
activity.solution:
p_d, sens, fpr = 0.01, 0.99, 0.05
p_pos = sens * p_d + fpr * (1 - p_d)
post = sens * p_d / p_pos
print(round(post, 3))
activity.hint: P(+) by total probability, then Bayes.

quiz.why: For independent events, P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B) = 0.3 × 0.5 = 0.15.
The prosecutor's fallacy swaps the two conditional probabilities: it treats P(evidence | innocent) as if it were P(innocent | evidence).
P(rain ∩ traffic) = P(traffic | rain) × P(rain) = 0.6 × 0.2 = 0.12.
There are 36 equally likely pairs, and 6 of them sum to 7: (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1). So 6/36 = 1/6.

scenes.text: A help desk gets on average 4 calls per minute. How likely are 8 or more in a minute?
The Poisson distribution answers it — and tells the manager how many agents to schedule.

steps.title: Discrete distributions
steps.body:
- **Binomial(n, p)**: number of successes in n independent trials. P(X = k) = C(n, k)pᵏ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ; mean np; variance np(1 − p).
- **Poisson(λ)**: counts of rare events in an interval. P(X = k) = e^(−λ)λᵏ/k!; mean = variance = λ.
- Bernoulli = Binomial(1, p); Geometric = trials until first success.

steps.title: Normal distribution
steps.body:
N(μ, σ²): symmetric bell curve. **Empirical rule**: ~68% within 1σ, ~95% within 2σ (1.96σ exactly), ~99.7% within 3σ.

Standardise: z = (x − μ)/σ and use z-tables: Φ(1) ≈ 0.841, Φ(1.645) ≈ 0.95, Φ(1.96) ≈ 0.975, Φ(2) ≈ 0.977.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using binomial when trials aren't independent or p changes (sampling without replacement from small populations → hypergeometric).
- Forgetting that Poisson variance equals its mean (over-dispersion signals a different model).
- Mixing up variance and standard deviation in z = (x − μ)/σ.

activity.prompt: Compute Binomial P(X = 3) for n = 10, p = 0.25 and Poisson P(X = 2) for λ = 4. Print both rounded to 3 decimals.
activity.starter:
import math
# b = ...
# po = ...
print(round(b, 3), round(po, 3))
activity.solution:
import math
b = math.comb(10, 3) * 0.25 ** 3 * 0.75 ** 7
po = math.exp(-4) * 4 ** 2 / math.factorial(2)
print(round(b, 3), round(po, 3))
activity.hint: math.comb for C(n,k); Poisson e^−λ λ^k / k!.

quiz.why: A binomial distribution has mean np = 20 × 0.3 = 6.
A binomial's variance is np(1 − p) = 20 × 0.3 × 0.7 = 4.2.
For a Poisson distribution, the variance equals the mean, so with λ = 3 the variance is 3.

quiz.q: About what % of normal data lies within 2σ?
quiz.why: By the empirical rule, about 68% of normal data lies within 1σ, 95% within 2σ and 99.7% within 3σ.

scenes.text: A survey of 1,000 voters finds 52% support a candidate. Is the race decided?
The 95% margin of error is about ±3.1 percentage points — the race is too close to call.

steps.title: Central limit theorem
steps.body: For a large enough sample (rule of thumb n ≥ 30), the **sample mean** is approximately normal with mean μ and **standard error SE = σ/√n**, whatever the population's shape (if variance is finite). For proportions: SE = √(p(1 − p)/n).

steps.title: Confidence intervals
steps.body:
- Mean, σ known: x̄ ± z*·σ/√n (z* = 1.96 for 95%, 1.645 for 90%, 2.576 for 99%).
- σ unknown: x̄ ± t*·s/√n with n − 1 degrees of freedom.
- Proportion: p̂ ± z*√(p̂(1 − p̂)/n).
- **Interpretation**: if we repeated the sampling many times, 95% of such intervals would contain the true value. It is *not* '95% probability the fixed true value is in this one interval' in the frequentist view.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using σ/n instead of σ/√n.
- Believing a bigger population needs a much bigger sample (margin depends mainly on n).
- Ignoring bias: a huge biased sample is still wrong (e.g. online-only polls).
- Misinterpreting the confidence level.

activity.prompt: Compute the 95% margin of error for p̂ = 0.52, n = 1000 and print it rounded to 3 decimals.
activity.starter:
import math
p, n = 0.52, 1000
# moe = 1.96 * sqrt(p(1-p)/n)
print(round(moe, 3))
activity.solution:
import math
p, n = 0.52, 1000
moe = 1.96 * math.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n)
print(round(moe, 3))

quiz.why: The standard error of the mean is σ/√n = 20/√100 = 20/10 = 2.

quiz.q: To halve the margin of error, n must…
quiz.why: The margin of error is proportional to 1/√n. To halve it you need √n to double, so n must quadruple.
For a two-sided 99% confidence interval the critical value is z* = 2.576. (1.96 is for 95% and 1.645 for 90%.)

quiz.q: When σ is unknown and n is small, use…
quiz.why: If σ is unknown and the sample is small, you estimate it from the data, which adds uncertainty, so the t distribution (wider tails) is used.

quiz.q: The CLT is about the distribution of…
quiz.why: The central limit theorem is about the sampling distribution of the sample mean: it becomes approximately normal for large n, whatever the population shape.

scenes.text: An e-commerce team tests a green 'Buy' button against the old blue one with 10,000 visitors each.
Conversion rises from 5.0% to 5.6%. A two-proportion test checks whether this could just be chance.

steps.title: The framework
steps.body:
- **H₀** (no effect) vs **H₁** (effect).
- Choose α (often 0.05) before looking.
- Compute a test statistic and its **p-value** = P(data at least this extreme | H₀ true).
- p ≤ α → reject H₀; otherwise 'fail to reject' (not 'prove H₀').
- **Type I error** (false positive) rate = α; **Type II** (false negative) = β; **power** = 1 − β.

steps.title: Which test?
steps.body:
- One mean, σ known → z-test; unknown → **one-sample t-test**.
- Two independent means → **two-sample (Welch) t-test**; paired before/after → paired t-test.
- Two proportions → two-proportion z-test.
- Categorical association → **chi-square test** χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E.
- Many groups' means → ANOVA.
- Non-normal small samples → Mann–Whitney, Wilcoxon.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. A/B.** p₁ = 0.050, p₂ = 0.056, n = 10,000 each. Pooled p = 0.053. SE = √(0.053·0.947·(2/10000)) ≈ 0.00317. z = 0.006/0.00317 ≈ **1.89** → two-sided p ≈ 0.059 > 0.05 → not significant at 5%.

**Example 2. Chi-square.** Observed [30, 20] vs expected [25, 25]: χ² = 25/25 + 25/25 = **2.0** (df = 1; critical 3.84 at α = 0.05) → not significant.

**Example 3. t-test.** n = 25, x̄ = 52, s = 5, H₀: μ = 50: t = 2/(5/5) = **2.0**; df 24, critical ≈ 2.064 → not significant two-sided.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'p = 0.03 means a 3% chance H₀ is true' — wrong.
- Peeking at A/B results daily and stopping when significant (inflates false positives).
- Running many tests without correction (multiple comparisons; use Bonferroni or control the false discovery rate).
- Confusing statistical significance with practical importance — report effect sizes and CIs.

activity.prompt: Compute the chi-square statistic for observed [30, 20] vs expected [25, 25] and print it.
activity.starter:
obs = [30, 20]
exp = [25, 25]
# chi2 = sum((o-e)^2/e)
print(chi2)
activity.solution:
obs = [30, 20]
exp = [25, 25]
chi2 = sum((o - e) ** 2 / e for o, e in zip(obs, exp))
print(chi2)

quiz.why: Each test has a 5% chance of a false positive, so the expected number across 20 tests is 20 × 0.05 = 1.

questions.q: Assertion: Doubling sample size halves the standard error. Reason: SE = σ/√n.
questions.why: The assertion is false: SE = σ/√n, so doubling n divides SE by √2 (about 1.41), not by 2. The reason is true.

The power of a test is 1 − β: the probability of detecting a real effect, that is of correctly rejecting a false H₀.

questions.q: Case: an A/B test is checked daily and stopped the first day p < 0.05. Problem?
questions.why: Stopping a test the first time p < 0.05 appears (optional stopping) gives many chances for a false positive and inflates the error rate. Fix the sample size in advance or use sequential methods.

questions.q: Case: a drug lowers BP by 0.3 mmHg with p = 0.0001 in 2 million people. Conclusion?
options: Statistically significant but likely clinically trivial
questions.why: With 2 million people even a tiny 0.3 mmHg effect gives a very small p-value. It is statistically significant but probably too small to matter clinically. Significance isn't importance.

story.title: Why are students dropping a course?

You plan the full analysis, then take the mock exam below.

steps.title: Plan
steps.body:
- Question: which factors are associated with dropping out by week 4?
- Data: enrolments, weekly activity logs, quiz scores, device type.
- Clean: de-duplicate students, parse dates, handle missing quiz scores.
